issues.legal_issue: An agricultural lease created by a mortgagee in possession binds the mortgagor after redemption only when it is a transaction that a prudent owner would make in the usual course of managing the property.
material_facts: The mortgagors had held the agricultural land as home-farm land, and it was entered as the mortgagees’ Khudkasht after the mortgage was made.
The mortgagees accepted the tenants’ written undertaking and received rent under it.
The rent fixed by the arrangement was not shown to be fair in light of the land’s likely net yield; comparison with the circle rate alone did not establish that it was reasonable.

The land was fertile, had canal irrigation, and was not shown to be an economic choice for leasing to tenants; the evidence did not establish exceptional grounds for the mortgagees’ decision to lease it.
After redemption, the mortgagors’ representatives sought possession, and the tenants claimed that the lease bound the owners.
issues.conclusion: The lease was not a prudent transaction in the usual course of management and did not bind the mortgagors after redemption.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a mortgagee in possession must manage the property as a person of ordinary prudence would manage their own property. Although a mortgagee’s agricultural lease may remain binding on the mortgagor after redemption, the party claiming that benefit must strictly establish that the lease was one a prudent owner would make in the usual course of management. The absence of a prohibition on leasing in the mortgage deed does not establish that the lease is binding. In Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh, the Court held that a lease prohibited by the mortgage deed is not binding; the Court explained that a lease not protected by section 76(a), or not bona fide, likewise does not bind the mortgagor.

predicates.appeal_challenges_binding_effect_of_agri: The proceeding challenges whether an agricultural lease remains binding on the owner after a mortgage is redeemed.
predicates.lease_created_by_mortgagee_in_possession: A mortgagee in possession created an agricultural lease over the mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgage_redeemed: The mortgagor or the mortgagor’s successor redeemed the mortgage.
predicates.lease_terms_were_not_shown_to_be_fair_ag: The party relying on the lease did not establish that its terms were fair in light of the income a prudent owner could obtain from the property.
predicates.lease_put_owner_protected_home_farm_inte: The lease put the owner’s interests in home-farm land at risk, and no exceptional grounds justified that action.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an agricultural lease made by a mortgagee in possession after redemption, the lease does not bind the mortgagor if its terms were not shown to be fair or it endangered protected home-farm interests without exceptional grounds.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming hereditary tenancy under a law that grants rights to persons who are tenants when the law commences must have been lawfully admitted as a tenant by someone authorized to admit them.
material_facts: The respondents claimed hereditary tenancy because they were in possession as tenants when the tenancy legislation commenced.
They had entered possession under an arrangement made with the mortgagees while the mortgagees were in possession.
The lease was not binding on the mortgagors because it was not a prudent transaction protected by section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
The mortgagees therefore lacked authority, as against the mortgagors, to admit the respondents as tenants under that lease.
issues.conclusion: The respondents did not acquire hereditary tenant rights against the mortgagors under section 29(a) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29(a) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939, confers hereditary tenancy rights on a person who is a tenant when the Act commences, which presupposes lawful tenancy. The claimant must have been admitted as a tenant by a person entitled to do so. A mortgagee in possession may admit a tenant if authorized by the mortgage deed or if the lease is protected by section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; an unauthorized lease cannot establish tenancy rights against the owner. In Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh, the Court held that a tenant under a lease not binding on the mortgagor does not acquire tenancy rights against the mortgagor. Jai Singh v. Munshi Singh did not apply because the lease there was found to be an ordinary course-of-management transaction.

predicates.claim_seeks_hereditary_tenancy_under_law: The proceeding involves a claim to hereditary tenancy under a law that grants rights to tenants at the law’s commencement.
predicates.claimant_was_in_possession_as_tenant_whe: The claimant was in possession, asserting tenancy, when the relevant law commenced.
predicates.claimant_was_admitted_only_under_mortgag: The claimant’s asserted tenancy arose only from an arrangement made by a mortgagee in possession.
predicates.mortgagee_lease_was_not_authorized_by_ow: The mortgagee had no authority from the owner to make the lease, and the lease was not a prudent management transaction binding on the owner.

issues.definition: A claimant who relies on a mortgagee’s unauthorized lease for hereditary tenancy rights at the commencement of the governing law acquires no such rights against the owner.
